title: Ecological patterns of variability in the life history of the European anchovy (Engraulis encrasicolus)
content:
Abstract

The study of life-history variability is crucial in evolutionary theory and ecology, especially for commercial species impacted by fishery pressure and climate change. The European anchovy (Engraulis encrasicolus) is a key commercial fish in the East Atlantic and Mediterranean regions. This study aimed to identify life-history trends in this species and evaluate how environmental factors influence its life-history parameters. A meta-analysis of data from 23 areas within the anchovy's native range included parameters such as maximum observed total length, maturation length, length at age 1 year, maximum age, asymptotic length and growth performance index. Three environmental factors were examined: sea surface temperature, net primary production and sea surface salinity. Findings revealed that anchovies in lower latitudes and warmer environments had smaller maximum and maturation sizes and lower early growth rate. Temperature exhibited significant negative correlation with maximum and maturation size, but regions with low salinity, such as the Azov-Black Sea basin, deviated from this pattern. There was no significant association between temperature and lifespan across the entire study range. The correlation between productivity and life-history parameters was least pronounced. Hence, these findings suggest that ongoing climate warming may decrease anchovy size. However, temperature's influence on life history involves trade-offs with both benefits and costs for adaptability, suggesting its effects are not universally consistent.
